div.head: Geþyncðo 2
div.ab: And gif ceorl geþeah, þæt he hæfde V hida fullice agenes landes, . . . bellan ⁊ burhgeat, setl ⁊ sundornote on cynges healle, þonne·wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes wyrðe.
⁊ gif ceorl geþeah, þæt he hæfde fullice fif hida agenes landes, cirican ⁊ ḱycenan, bellhus ⁊ burhgeat, setl ⁊ sundernote on cynges healle, þonne wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes weorðe.
Et si uillanus excreuisset, ut haberet plenarie quinque hidas terrę suę proprię, ęcclesiam et coquinam, timpanarium et ianuam, sedem et sundernotam in aula regis, deinceps erat taini lege dignus.

[60, 1] Et si uillanus ita creuisset sua probitate, quod pleniter haberet quinque hídas de suo próprio alodio et ęcclesiam propriam et clocarium et coquinam et portam, sedem et priuatum profectum in aula regis, tunc deinde erat dignus honore liberalitatis, quod Angli dicunt þegenscipes þurðe.
And gif ceorl geþeah þæt he hæfde fullice fif hida agenes landes, cirican and kycenan, bellhus and burhgeat, setl and sundernote on cynges healle, þonne wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes weorðe.

Und wenn ein Gemeinfreier [so] emporkam, dass er völlig 5 Hiden eigenen Landes hatte, Kirche und Küche, Glockenhaus (Glocke D) und Burgthor, Sitz und besonderes Amt in des Königs Halle, dann genoss er hinfort Thegnberechtigung.

And if a ceorl prospered [so] that he fully had 5 hides of his own land, a church and a kitchen, a bell-house (bell, D) and a burh-gate [a fortified manor, more than a mere farmstead in the village], a seat and a special office in the king's hall, then he was henceforth entitled to thegn-right.

And if a ceorl prospered, that he possessed fully five hides of land of his own, a bell and a castle-gate, a seat and special office in the king’s hall, then was he henceforth entitled to the rights of a thegn.

And if a commoner prospered so that he had fully five hides of his own property with a church and kitchen, a bell house and fortified gate, a seat and an appointed role in the king’s hall, then he was worthy of a thane’s rights ever after.

note.label: in line with
note.quote: The wergild here equates to that of a thane in clause 5, thus bringing the clauses on social promotion in this text in line with those in On the Ranks of People and Law above, especially clause 2.

div.note: D lacks ‘cirican ⁊ kycenan’. Stevenson (with Coote) divides ‘cirican ⁊ kycenan | bellhus ⁊ b. | s. ⁊ s. | on’; the reading ‘burhgeatsetl’ (since Price–Thorpe) is ruled out by the MSS, which punctuate before ‘s’, by the Latin versions and by the rhythm. Liebermann compares Norðleod 7 ff. and Geþyncðo 3, Grið 21.1.; U: checked against Whitelock, EHD I (1979), and corrected (before: ‘And if a ceorl prospered, that he possessed fully five hides of land of his own, a bell and a castle-gate, a seat and a special office in the king's hall, then was he henceforth entitled to the rights of a thegn.’).

five hides: One hide is equivalent to the amount of land a single plowman could till in one day. During the Old English period, depending on region, one hide could equate to an area ranging from 60 to 180 acres, though it was standardized following the Conquest to roughly 120 acres. The five-hide unit seems to have been a common standard of measurement in Old English law and may have indicated the threshold above which a landowner owed military obligations to the king.

Die Anfänge von 2. 3. 5. 6. 7 lauten wie die von Norðleod 7. 7, 1. 8. 10. 11. 12; letztere Sätze rühren also wohl vom selben Verf. her.—Das Präteritum þeah könnte zwar von þicgean ‘erreichen, empfangen, nehmen’ herkommen; und geþicð se æðeling to cynesetle sagt Ælfric Hom. ed. Thorpe I 110. Allein Verf. meint þéon, geþogen, geþuge 4. 7 und geþeod, geþeo(n) Norðleod 7—12

The beginnings of 2. 3. 5. 6. 7 read like those of Norðleod 7. 7, 1. 8. 10. 11. 12; the latter sentences therefore probably derive from the same author.—The preterite þeah could indeed come from þicgean ‘reach, receive, take’; and Ælfric Hom. ed. Thorpe I 110 says geþicð se æðeling to cynesetle. But the author means þéon, geþogen, geþuge 4. 7 and geþeod, geþeo(n) Norðleod 7—12

Vgl. Gl Fünf Hufen; zu Inst: Allod. Denke aus Norðleod 9 hinzu: ‘zur Staatslast eingeschätzt’; es liegt dies im Worte ‘eigen’: durch den Besitzer, nicht durch einen Oberherrn dem Staate gegenüber vertreten
Cf. Gl Fünf Hufen; on Inst: Allod. Supply from Norðleod 9: ‘assessed for the public burden’; this is implied in the word ‘own’: represented vis-à-vis the state by the owner, not by an overlord

Diese Nebenbedingungen entsprachen zwar vermutlich zumeist den wirklichen tatsächlichen Zuständen. M. a. W.: regelmässig besass wohl jeder Thegn Haushalt, Kapelle, Hallengericht und, was schon schwerer vorstellbar, eine amtliche Beziehung zum Königshofe (die kriegerische Pflicht ist offenbar nicht oder nicht allein gemeint); allein dass dies je rechtliche Bedingungen zur Standeserhöhung waren, ist schwer denkbar.—Vgl. Gl Eigenkirche 2. b

These subsidiary conditions probably did, for the most part, correspond to the real, actual circumstances. In other words: every thegn probably regularly possessed a household, chapel, hall-court and — what is already harder to imagine — an official connection with the king’s court (military duty is evidently not meant, or not alone); but that these were ever legal conditions for elevation in rank is hard to conceive.—Cf. Gl Eigenkirche 2. b

Ebd. Küche. Darunter vielleicht mitverstanden hält Bennett (Hist. of cornmilling bei Köhne Mühle in Beitr. z. Gschi. Technik V [1913] 36) Backofen und Mühle (s. o. zu Gerefa 16⁸), möglicherweise samt dem Zwange, der die Gutsinsassen verband, dort zu backen und zu mahlen

Ibid. Küche. Bennett (Hist. of cornmilling, in Köhne Mühle in Beitr. z. Gschi. Technik V [1913] 36) thinks oven and mill are perhaps included under it (see above on Gerefa 16⁸), possibly together with the compulsion that bound the inhabitants of the estate to bake and grind there

‘Glockenhaus’ ist archetyp, da neben der Klasse hq auch in I; vgl. cloecarium : bellhus Ælfric Gloss. ed. Zupitza 314; Gl Glocke 3. [Auch Taranger Angelsaks. Kirk. 252, obwohl er das besondere Glockenhaus neben der Kirche betont, lässt die Frage offen, ob die Glocke nur kirchlich diente. Sie war (neben Siegel und Kasse) Symbol politischer Verkörperung in Französischen Städten 12. Jhs.; ebenso bezeichnet belle et burgiet die Immunität fürs Herrschaftsgut; s. Gl Burgtor 2a. Hickes nimmt ‘portam cum clocario’ als Hendiadyoin

‘Bell-house’ belongs to the archetype, since it occurs in I as well as in the class hq; cf. cloecarium : bellhus Ælfric Gloss. ed. Zupitza 314; Gl Glocke 3. [Taranger Angelsaks. Kirk. 252, too, although he stresses the separate bell-house beside the church, leaves open the question whether the bell served only church purposes. It was (along with seal and treasury) a symbol of political corporate identity in French towns of the 12th cent.; likewise belle et burgiet denotes the immunity of the lordly estate; see Gl Burgtor 2a. Hickes takes ‘portam cum clocario’ as a hendiadys
burh: befestigtes Domänengehöft, mehr als blosser Bauernhof im Dorfe; vgl. S. 445f; 454 vorletzte Zeile
burh: a fortified demesne farmstead, more than a mere peasant farm in the village; cf. p. 445f; 454 last line but one

S. o. S. 230 Pax⁶. Sweet erklärt ‘lawcourt held at citygate’; aber von einer Stadt ist hier keine Rede, sondern vom Haupthaus des Manor, das oft burg (s. d. Gl) heisst: ‘Die Herrenhaustür (und nicht ‘Städtetor’) erbricht der Pflanze und Tier schädigende Schnee’ im Gedicht Salomo 306 ed. Vincenti 71. Nicht gemeint ist ‘Erhaltung und Verteidigung eines Tors in der Grafschafts-Hauptstadt, etwa samt Zoll-Einnahme’

See above p. 230 Pax⁶. Sweet explains ‘lawcourt held at citygate’; but there is no question here of a town, rather of the chief house of the manor, which is often called burg (see that word in Gl): ‘The snow that harms plant and beast breaks open the manor-house door (and not ‘city gate’)’ in the poem Salomo 306 ed. Vincenti 71. What is not meant is ‘the maintenance and defence of a gate in the county town, perhaps together with the toll revenue’

Technisch: ‘bestimmter Platz als Würdenzeichen’; setl kann ‘gesellschaftliche Stellung’ heissen (Toller). Auch hierzu denkt ‘in Königshalle’ hinzu Stevenson EHR 1897, 490. Vielleicht verbinden sich wie in vor. Z.⁵ die zwei alliterierenden Wörter zu Einem Begriffe: ‘Amtssitz’

Technically: ‘a definite place as a mark of dignity’; setl can mean ‘social position’ (Toller). Here too Stevenson EHR 1897, 490 supplies ‘in the king’s hall’. Perhaps, as in the preceding line⁵, the two alliterating words combine into a single concept: ‘seat of office’
Königsdienst (s. d. Gl 4. 5) erhebt zu höherem Range
Royal service (see that word in Gl 4. 5) raises a man to higher rank
Laut Norðleod 11 wird der Adelsrang erblich, sobald Vater, Sohn und Eukel Thegn (s. d. Gl 11) gewesen; s. Gl Gefolgsadel 4d
According to Norðleod 11 noble rank becomes hereditary as soon as father, son and grandson have been thegns (see that word in Gl 11); see Gl Gefolgsadel 4d
